analysis.one_liner: Gives overburdened communities stronger legal tools against pollution and requires polluters to prove permits won't harm them.
analysis.headline: The bill won support from 105 House Democrats but died in committee without a single hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Civil Rights Act so people could sue over pollution that hits communities of color harder, even without proof of intent, and could recover attorney fees. It would require air and water pollution permits to account for all pollution already in a neighborhood, and to be denied or tightened if regulators cannot be reasonably certain of no harm. It also adds federal agency environmental justice duties, new advisory bodies, park-access grants, and labeling rules for cosmetics and menstrual products.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of low-income neighborhoods, communities of color, and tribal and Indigenous areas that sit next to highways, refineries, chemical plants, and waste sites. They would gain a private right to sue over discriminatory pollution impacts, a say in federal projects that could add to their exposure, and grants for parks, transit-to-trails access, and safer alternatives to toxic products. Fossil-fuel-dependent workers would also get transition assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities of color near polluting facilities

how_it_helps.text: Amends Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to bar federally funded activities from causing disparate impacts on the basis of race, color, or national origin, and gives any aggrieved person the right to sue in federal court, with attorney's fees recoverable for disparate-impact claims [S2][S3].

Amends the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act so that major-source permits must account for cumulative impacts of all pollution in the area, and no permit may be issued or renewed unless there is a reasonable certainty of no harm to the health of nearby residents, including for applicants with a record of persistent violations [S3].

Requires federal agencies proposing actions that could affect an environmental justice community to prepare a community impact report covering cumulative exposure, alternatives developed by the affected community, and impacts on parks and energy prices [S3].

Creates grant programs for park access in urban areas, a transit-to-trails program for underserved communities, and research and grants on safer chemical alternatives in cosmetics, baby products, and menstrual products, plus labeling requirements for those products [S2][S3].
Directs transition assistance and economic revitalization for fossil fuel-dependent communities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities with air and water discharge permits, including refineries, chemical plants, manufacturers, and waste handlers, would face stricter permitting, denial of permits, and additional controls. Any entity receiving federal funds, including universities, hospitals, and local governments, would face disparate-impact litigation exposure. Taxpayers fund the new grant programs, advisory bodies, and agency reporting duties.

drawbacks.text: Permitting applicants would bear the burden of showing a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' for whole communities, a much stricter standard than current law, which could delay or block new plants, refineries, and infrastructure projects and their jobs [S3].

A private right of action on a disparate-impact standard would expose a wide range of federal-fund recipients, including schools, hospitals, and local governments, to litigation costs, and disputes over permit denials and cumulative-impact analyses would likely generate extended legal fights [S3].

The bill creates many new advisory councils, agency strategies, scorecards, and reporting requirements whose administrative costs and effectiveness were never examined in a hearing, and grant programs like the park fund require 100 percent local matching funds that struggling communities may not have [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living with stacked pollution burdens, the bill's core trade is real legal power and cleaner permits in exchange for slower, costlier, and more litigated permitting. The civil-rights fix and cumulative-impact review address a genuine, documented gap in current law, but the wide scope of the bill, the number of new institutions it creates, and its strict burden-shifting standard would carry significant compliance and litigation costs that critics were never given the chance to argue on the floor. Its backers never had to defend those costs in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to six House committees at once, but none of the committees held a hearing or markup and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2023 by Rep. Raúl Grijalva and named for the late Rep. A. Donald McEachin, and gathered 105 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3][S4].

It was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, and Education and the Workforce, with parts sent to five subcommittees [S1][S5].
No committee reported the bill, no hearings or markups appear in the action history, and the bill never received a House or Senate vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Polluting industries and permit applicants kept the current rules, which do not require cumulative-impact reviews or give residents a private right to sue over discriminatory pollution impacts. Members who faced no floor vote never had to answer for a position.

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors

for.name: 105 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all from one party

against.name: Chairs of six House committees (Republican majority)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral but scheduled no hearings or markups in two years

against.name: House leadership (118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: All 105 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill went nowhere without them.

industries.industry: Refineries, chemical plants, and other major air and water polluters
industries.note: They would face cumulative-impact permitting, permit denials, tighter controls, and a plan requirement for persistent violators. Neighborhoods near these facilities would get cleaner air and water as a result.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and importers of cosmetics, menstrual, and consumer products
industries.note: New ingredient-labeling requirements and research into safer alternatives would raise compliance costs, while consumers gain disclosure about ingredients in products they use daily.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel companies and fossil-fuel-dependent communities
industries.note: The bill directs transition assistance and economic revitalization to workers and towns dependent on fossil fuel jobs, even as stricter permitting squeezes the industry itself.

industries.industry: Environmental justice organizations and community groups
industries.note: New grant programs, ombuds and advisory roles, and technical assistance would fund and formalize their participation in permitting and agency decisions.

industries.industry: Recipients of federal funding (local governments, universities, hospitals)
industries.note: Expanded Title VI disparate-impact liability and a private right of action create litigation exposure, though the same tool would let residents challenge discriminatory pollution from funded activities.
